ratings.plot: Based on a true story, primarily on a conflict between two youth gangs, a 14-year-old boy's girlfriend conflicts with the head of one gang for an unclear reason, until finally the conflict comes to a violent climax.

verdict.reason: Edward Yang's four-hour masterpiece about teenage gang warfare and doomed love demands the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes this rare New York showing essential.

ratings.plot: The eldest daughter of a broken and troubled family works to keep the family together and look after her younger siblings, who are slipping into a life of crime.

verdict.reason: Essential Hou at a major venue—a restored restoration of one of cinema's great films about family fracture and moral compromise. The DCP at Metrograph is how to see this.

ratings.plot: A young couple leave their mining town home for Taipei where they struggle to eke out a living in an industrial wasteland.

verdict.reason: Hsiao-Hsien Hou's essential work on urban alienation demands the theater. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes this 1986 masterpiece luminous and immediate.

ratings.plot: All the while, Master Chu tries to find his place in the foreign American world.

verdict.reason: Ang Lee's debut is a rare repertory screening at Metrograph. The film moves with visual clarity and warmth through the collision of tradition and assimilation.

ratings.plot: Things go wrong for a high ranking mobster when he doesn't follow his boss's orders.

verdict.reason: Kim Jee-woon's crime masterpiece deserves a theater. The DCP restoration at Metrograph makes the violent elegance sing.

ratings.plot: In Mumbai, Nurse Prabha's routine is troubled when she receives an unexpected gift from her estranged husband. Her younger roommate, Anu, tries in vain to find a spot in the city to be intimate with her boyfriend.

verdict.reason: Watch it. Kapadia's debut is a precise, patient film about two women in Mumbai finding small moments of freedom, shot with rare visual clarity on 35mm.

ratings.plot: Ryuichi Sakamoto's last performance, a concert film featuring just him and his piano playing for the last time before passing away.

verdict.reason: A final document of one of music's great minds at the piano—this is not a concert film you can replace with a recording. Neo Sora captures something sacred in the space between Sakamoto and his instrument that demands the theater's acoustic presence.

ratings.plot: K2's first winter ascent claimed 5 lives, revealing modern alpinism's struggles with commercialization, social media impact, and conflicts between marginalized climbers and traditional elites.

verdict.reason: Amir Bar-Lev's documentary about K2's first winter ascent is essential viewing on the specific stakes of modern mountaineering. The film captures a real tragedy that exposes class fracture and commercial pressure in extreme sport, best witnessed in a theater where the altitude and moral weight can breathe.

ratings.plot: A handsome prince rides a flying horse to faraway lands and embarks on magical adventures, which include befriending a witch, meeting Aladdin, battling demons and falling in love with a princess.

verdict.reason: The oldest surviving narrative feature film and a silent masterpiece of silhouette animation—see it on the big screen at Film Forum where the delicate cutout artistry registers as intended. Reiniger's intricate frame-by-frame craftsmanship and fluid character movement hold up because the aesthetic was never about technical flash, just pure visual storytelling.

ratings.plot: Misael lives as an independent logger in the woods, enjoying his solitary freedom. When he must care for his older sister, his peaceful existence is upended and the foundations of his carefully constructed life begin to fall apart.

verdict.reason: Lisandro Alonso's meditative work on solitude and obligation deserves the big screen. A 100-minute Lincoln Center screening of a director working at full precision.

ratings.plot: A glimpse at the lives of two petty criminals in Taipei.

verdict.reason: Hou Hsiao-hsien's 1996 masterpiece demands a theater and a full two hours of attention. The 116-minute rhythm and Taipei street photography are built for the big screen.

ratings.plot: A group of high school students sets off on a school trip to discover the ruins of Pompeii. They are seized by a sense of vertigo. They allow themselves to be overwhelmed by desire and anger, until they surrender completely.

verdict.reason: A rare film about teenage intoxication and desire shot with real formal ambition at one of New York's premier venues. Atlan uses Pompeii's stasis to frame how adolescent bodies move through space and surrender to impulse, and the 16mm cinematography catches light the way memory does.

movies.title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem

ratings.plot: A decade post-death, filmmaker William Greaves reveals his final work: footage of a 1972 gathering he arranged with Harlem Renaissance legends, which he deemed his most significant capture.

verdict.reason: A posthumous William Greaves film showing archival footage of Harlem Renaissance figures from 1972 is a rare historical document that belongs on the big screen. Lincoln Center is the only venue, and this is the kind of cinema history that dissolves into the ether if you skip the theater run.

ratings.plot: Four strangers' paths cross by chance, leading to complex emotional entanglements that challenge their existing relationships and force them to confront uncomfortable truths about love and commitment.

verdict.reason: Lee Chang-dong's first film in a decade demands the big screen and your full attention. Nearly three hours of moral complexity and emotional precision—see it before word spreads.

ratings.plot: Rose, a German widow, hides from Russian soldiers who like to rape women and fights off Polish refugees who will steal everything she has. She gets help when Tadeusz, a former Polish officer, arrives looking to hide from his past.

verdict.reason: A harrowing 90-minute film about survival in post-war chaos that earns its moral weight without sentimentality. Smarzowski's unflinching direction and the confined setting make this a punishing but necessary theatrical experience.

ratings.plot: A criminal on the run hides in a circus and seeks to possess the daughter of the ringmaster at any cost.

verdict.reason: Browning's strangest masterpiece belongs on the big screen, and Lincoln Center's print restores the full grotesque power of a silent film that still shocks. Lon Chaney's performance—playing an armless criminal who manipulates desire itself—is the kind of physical storytelling that only works in a theater.

ratings.plot: A notorious prison, an invisible force starts killing inmates brutally, compelling enemy gangs and corrupt guards to work together as they try to survive the mounting bloodshed.

verdict.reason: Joko Anwar blends horror, dark comedy, and prison tension into something genuinely new. A perfect fit for Alamo Drafthouse—weird, brutal, and best seen with an audience.

ratings.plot: In secret conversations on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night, the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza are revealed by the people who designed and operated them.

verdict.reason: Watch this essential documentary on Gaza now while it's in theaters. Israeli insiders speaking on Tel Aviv rooftops offer rare testimony about calculated systems of killing.

ratings.plot: Thirty-four days before she’s sent to prison, notorious Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes invites a skeptical film crew to document her every move. What begins as an intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss. From boundary-pushing directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim comes YOU CAN SEE EVERYTHING.

verdict.reason: Nathan Fielding and Lance Oppenheim have made something genuinely disorienting about power, performance, and the camera's complicity—a three-hour document that earns its runtime. The film's structural ambition (letting Holmes control her own image while the filmmakers undermine it) is best experienced on the big screen where the manipulation becomes tactile.

ratings.plot: A young Buenos Aires mother finds employment as a sex worker and struggles to live under the same laws that are supposed to protect her.

verdict.reason: A rare screening of a perfectly pitched 82-minute film about systemic injustice. Berneri's direction cuts clean and does not waste a frame.

ratings.plot: Soon after a stranger arrives in a little village, a mysterious sickness starts spreading. A policeman, drawn into the incident, is forced to solve the mystery in order to save his daughter...

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical return of Na Hong-jin's masterwork—mystery and dread that deepens with every viewing. The 156-minute runtime demands a big screen and Metrograph's DCP projection.

ratings.plot: A portrait of genius music composer Ryuichi Sakamoto.

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical screening of one of the essential music documentaries of the decade. Schible captures Sakamoto's final creative period with intimate access and formal sophistication that demands a big screen and proper sound.

movies.title: The Taking of Pelham One Two Three

ratings.plot: Four armed men hijack a New York City subway car and demand a ransom for the passengers. The city's police are faced with a conundrum: Even if it's paid, how could they get away?

verdict.reason: See this '70s masterclass in procedural tension on the big screen. The 35mm print at Metrograph restores every detail of the subway car and the city streets above it.

ratings.plot: A high-strung news producer finds herself in a love triangle between a talented but self-doubting reporter and a charming new anchor, who embodies the growing trivialization of news that she is determined to fight against.

verdict.reason: One of the sharpest films about journalism, ambition, and the cost of principle — see it restored at Metrograph while it plays. Holly Hunter's performance is a masterclass in conveying intelligence and heartbreak through restraint.

ratings.plot: A psychopath tries to forcibly persuade a tennis star to agree to his theory that two strangers can get away with murder by submitting to his plan to kill the other's most-hated person.

verdict.reason: Hitchcock's masterpiece of psychological manipulation deserves the big screen. The 35mm print at Metrograph shows why the geometry of his shot-making still cuts.

ratings.plot: A young African-American man grapples with his identity and sexuality while experiencing the everyday struggles of childhood, adolescence, and burgeoning adulthood.

verdict.reason: Watch it—a genuine masterpiece about identity and belonging that demands the big screen. Barry Jenkins' direction transforms intimate moments into something transcendent.

ratings.plot: An executive of a Yokohama shoe company becomes a victim of extortion when his chauffeur's son is kidnapped by mistake and held for ransom.

verdict.reason: One of Kurosawa's sharpest films about class and moral compromise — essential on 35mm at Metrograph. The architectural compositions of Tokyo's vertical city are designed for the theatrical frame, and the second half's procedural intensity builds to a knockout final act.

ratings.plot: Portrait of a middle-class family in Taipei. A man in his forties, his teenage daughter and his eight-year-old son experience life, navigating between remorse, hope and disappointment.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for Edward Yang's three-hour masterpiece on family life and time's passage. Metrograph's DCP restoration honors the precision of Yang's composition and color.

ratings.plot: A young couple trying for a baby moves into an aging, ornate apartment building on Central Park West, where they find themselves surrounded by peculiar neighbors.

verdict.reason: One of the great films about paranoia and violation—see it on 35mm at Metrograph. Polanski's control of suspense and performance from Mia Farrow make this essential.

movies.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother

ratings.plot: Follows Latif, a devoutly religious hitman, who embarks on a desperate journey across Houston to protect his children after his wife dies, confronting forces closing in and beliefs threatening to unravel.

verdict.reason: A rare 97% film that explores faith and fatherhood through crime drama—worth the trip. Angelika is showing it on 35mm, the format Tariq shot it for.

ratings.plot: Fifteen years after murdering his sister on Halloween night 1963, Michael Myers escapes from a mental hospital and returns to the small town of Haddonfield, Illinois, to kill again.

verdict.reason: Carpenter's lean, methodical filmmaking defined the slasher template and still works as pure cinema. Ninety-one minutes of sustained dread—every frame counts, no fat.

ratings.plot: A young woman seeks to break a curse by raising $1000 for psychics in a pre-millennium alternate universe. She navigates the seedy underbelly of Trashtown via scooter, encountering bizarre characters along the way.

verdict.reason: Watch it: a sharp comedy-fantasy that finds humor in desperation and the absurd. Sriram's DCP debut at Anthology has the wildness and precision that justify the trip.

ratings.plot: This Hong Kong-set crime drama follows the lives of a hitman, hoping to get out of the business, and his elusive female partner.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai at peak form deserves a big screen. The DCP restoration at Metrograph lets you see the neon architecture and visual excess that made this film matter.

ratings.plot: A research chemist comes under personal and professional attack when he decides to appear in a 60 Minutes exposé on Big Tobacco.

verdict.reason: Michael Mann's 157-minute corporate thriller is essential on 35mm, where the tense editing and meticulous framing of power dynamics come into full focus. Russell Crowe's performance as a man systematically destroyed for telling the truth remains one of the great portraits of professional conscience in American cinema.

ratings.plot: As World War II and the German occupation ends, the Polish resistance and the Soviet forces turn on each other in an attempt to take over leadership in Communist Poland.

verdict.reason: Essential Polish cinema at one of New York's best venues. Wajda's 1958 masterpiece about resistance and betrayal in occupied Poland remains urgent and formally alive.

ratings.plot: Odysseus, king of Ithaca, embarks on a perilous journey to return home after the Trojan War.

verdict.reason: Nolan's 172-minute epic demands the 70mm experience at Lincoln Square or elsewhere. This is the rare theatrical event where format matters as much as the film itself.

ratings.plot: Karsten apparently has it settled. However, in this provincial German town, a moment of weakness turns to disaster, disappointment soon fuels anger, justice hides behind hypocrisy, and evil gradually unfolds.

verdict.reason: A rare screening of this sharp moral drama at Lincoln Center. Özge builds tension from small-town hypocrisy with precision that rewards full attention.

ratings.plot: After enduring years of malfunctioning products, Wile E. Coyote teams up with a local personal injury attorney to take on ACME, the manufacturer of anything and everything used by the Looney Tunes characters.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for a Looney Tunes film that actually lands the joke. Dave Green finds real comedy in the lawsuit premise instead of coasting on nostalgia.

ratings.plot: At Westerburg High where cliques rule, jocks dominate and all the popular girls are named Heather, it's going to take a Veronica and mysterious new kid to give teen angst a body count.

verdict.reason: One of the sharpest satires of American high school ever made—caustic, funny, and structurally airtight in ways most comedies aren't. Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see the production design and framing that make Lehmann's staging as precise as the script.

ratings.plot: While a zombie virus breaks out in South Korea, passengers struggle to survive on the train from Seoul to Busan.

verdict.reason: A genre film with real momentum and heart—see it on the big screen at Metrograph. Yeon Sang-ho traps character and chaos in one metal tube and never lets the pressure drop.

ratings.plot: "The Washington Post" reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein uncover the details of the Watergate scandal that leads to President Richard Nixon's resignation.

verdict.reason: Essential political thriller that defined the genre and still moves like a freight train. Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see the craftsmanship in every frame.

ratings.plot: An aging widower arranges a marriage for his only daughter.

verdict.reason: Ozu's final film deserves the big screen, especially in restoration. The DCP at Metrograph lets you see the geometric precision of his compositions as intended.

ratings.plot: A modern adaptation of the classic Greek tragedy which falls within a social realism. To the law of men, the young Antigone apposes her own sets of values.

verdict.reason: Deraspe's modern retelling of the Greek tragedy cuts deeper than the source material, turning family loyalty and state power into a collision that feels urgent and alive. Metrograph is showing it on 35mm, which gives the social realism texture and grain that streaming will flatten.

ratings.plot: Meeting a stranger in a railway station, a woman is tempted to cheat on her husband.

verdict.reason: Lean's masterpiece of restraint and desire demands the big screen. Metrograph's 35mm print restores every glance and silent ache.

ratings.plot: In 19th century Massachusetts, the March sisters--Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy--on the threshold of womanhood, go through many ups and downs in life and endeavor to make important decisions about their futures.

verdict.reason: Gerwig's take on this story justifies the trip, especially on Metrograph's screen. The 135-minute runtime and formal precision reward theatrical attention.

ratings.plot: When a nobleman is threatened by a family curse on his newly inherited estate, detective Sherlock Holmes is hired to investigate.

verdict.reason: Terence Fisher's 1959 take is the definitive Sherlock adaptation on screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes this the night to catch it.

ratings.plot: In 2006, To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen sets out to make television history.

verdict.reason: Lance Oppenheim makes a sharp film about the messy reality behind a TV sensation that defined an era. The 110-minute runtime moves fast, and the subject—how Hansen's crusade became theater—has teeth that justify the theatrical experience.
A rare screening at Lincoln Center of a film with near-universal praise. See it on the big screen while you can.

ratings.plot: Two best friends become stranded on the mystical world of Nakali, where their only escape might cost them their shared lifetime of memories.

verdict.reason: Skip the streaming queue and catch this one theatrically—the animation design demands a big screen and the emotional core about friendship and sacrifice lands harder in a theater full of people. The 109-minute runtime moves fast enough to hold attention, and the world-building rewards the full theatrical experience.

ratings.plot: Assigned to a county-mandated drug court program, Cody Parsons embarks on the tenuous journey toward recovery amidst the opioid epidemic in rural Ohio.

verdict.reason: A serious film about addiction and recovery that earns its emotional weight without sentimentality. Adam Meeks directs with a steady hand that lets the performances and the specificity of rural Ohio speak for themselves.

ratings.plot: To satisfy his nagging parents, a gay landlord and a female tenant agree to a marriage of convenience, but his parents arrive to visit and things get out of hand.

verdict.reason: Ang Lee's debut is a smart comedy that earns its emotional turns without losing its edge. Metrograph is showing it on 35mm.

movies.title: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown

ratings.plot: A television actress encounters a variety of eccentric characters after embarking on a journey to discover why her lover abruptly left her.

verdict.reason: Essential Almodóvar on 35mm at Metrograph. The 1988 restoration glows on film; this is how the color and rhythm were meant to land.

movies.title: The Flavor of Green Tea Over Rice

ratings.plot: A childless middle-aged couple faces a marital crisis.

verdict.reason: Essential Ozu on 35mm at Metrograph. A masterwork about marriage and compromise that demands the big screen.

ratings.plot: Three amateur robbers plan to hold up a Brooklyn bank. A nice, simple robbery: Walk in, take the money, and run. Unfortunately, the supposedly uncomplicated heist suddenly becomes a bizarre nightmare as everything that could go wr...

verdict.reason: One of the essential New York films, a masterwork of tension and character that demands the big screen. IFC Center is showing a 35mm print of Lumet's 1975 classic, the only way to see it done right.

ratings.plot: Haru and Luis love competing in Tokyo's ballroom dance scene, but after tragedy strikes, Haru withdraws into isolation. When friends coax her back to the studio, she develops an infatuation with the new instructor.

verdict.reason: Josef Kubota Wladyka makes films that find genuine emotion in specificity, and a 122-minute comedy-drama about Tokyo's ballroom dance world earning this level of regard suggests real craft. The setting and the focus on how dance becomes a path back from grief gives this genuine theatrical weight.

movies.title: If I Go Will They Miss Me

ratings.plot: A boy sees ghostly figures of other boys in his neighborhood while grappling with his father's distance. These visions uncover hidden connections between them and their shared heritage.

verdict.reason: A debut feature that earns its acclaim through precise observation of grief and inheritance rather than sentiment. Walter Thompson-Hernandez builds the supernatural around a boy's longing for his father with the restraint of someone who understands that the uncanny works best when rooted in real emotional distance.

ratings.plot: A study of the lives and romantic entanglements of various interconnected women.

verdict.reason: Cukor's 1939 ensemble comedy is essential cinema—a rare theatrical return of a master work. The all-female cast and bitingly sharp dialogue deserve the big screen at Film Forum.

movies.title: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma

ratings.plot: A director making a slasher sequel becomes obsessed with casting the original film's 'final girl,' leading both women into psychological and sexual chaos.

verdict.reason: Schoenbrun's metafictional horror-comedy justifies the trip on 35mm. The premise—a director chasing an actress into psychological obsession—plays sharper on a big screen.

ratings.plot: A woman who agrees to a deal to help an old acquaintance. She follows the hero on his adventure and enters dangerous territory where she is then confronted with her own desire.

verdict.reason: Valeska Grisebach's first action film deserves the big screen at Lincoln Center. A 167-minute immersion in desire and danger from a director working at the height of her powers.

ratings.plot: After earning a licence to kill, secret agent James Bond sets out on his first mission as 007. Bond must defeat a private banker funding terrorists in a high-stakes game of poker at Casino Royale, in Montenegro.

verdict.reason: Essential Bond film that redefined the franchise with real stakes and tension. Martin Campbell's direction and the poker sequence are worth the big screen.

ratings.plot: The Weight, portrays the life of Jung(Cho Jae-Huyn) who grew up as an orphan and was adopted into a family of only a mother and a son. Jung is now a hunchback man due to scoliosis and is a live-in mortician taking care of corpses ...

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical screening of a quietly devastating South Korean drama that earns its emotional power through restraint and specificity. Jeon Kyu-hwan's direction finds profound dignity in the small gestures of a mortician's daily work, and the film's refusal to sentimentalize makes every moment land harder.

ratings.plot: After the devastating events of Avengers: Infinity War (2018), the universe is in ruins. With the help of remaining allies, the Avengers assemble once more in order to reverse Thanos' actions and restore balance to the universe.

verdict.reason: A three-hour blockbuster that justifies its runtime with payoff for a decade of storytelling. IMAX or 4DX amplifies the scale.

ratings.plot: Georges and Anne are an octogenarian couple. They are cultivated, retired music teachers. Their daughter, also a musician, lives in Britain with her family. One day, Anne has a stroke, and the couple's bond of love is severely tes...

verdict.reason: Haneke's masterpiece about time, decline, and devotion demands the big screen and your full attention. Metrograph's 35mm print honors the film's precise, unflinching direction.

ratings.plot: While on a trip to Paris with his fiancée's family, a nostalgic screenwriter finds himself mysteriously going back to the 1920s every day at midnight.

verdict.reason: Allen's best work in years—a romantic fantasy that earns its charm without straining. The 35mm print at Metrograph restores the cinematography to what it should be.

movies.title: Once Upon a Time in China II

ratings.plot: Arriving by train in Guangzhou, 1895, the trio fight off White Lotus followers, who want to kill all foreigners and the cute, European dressed 13th Aunt. It's not kung fu master Dr. Wong's (Jet Li) last fight.

verdict.reason: Essential Tsui action cinema with Jet Li at peak form. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes the fight choreography sing on the big screen.

ratings.plot: On a remote Scottish isle, siblings Isla and Sandy hunt birds and talk to mythical beings while fighting off outsiders. Their lives change when Daniel, an awkward official, arrives to relocate them.

verdict.reason: A debut feature that finds real comedy in isolation, strangeness, and the collision between community myth and bureaucratic intrusion. Louis Paxton's command of tone and landscape—mixing deadpan Scottish humor with genuinely surreal moments—rewards full attention on a theater screen.

ratings.plot: An upper-class widow falls in love with a much younger, down-to-earth nurseryman, much to the disapproval of her children and criticism of her country club peers.

verdict.reason: Sirk's melodrama remains essential—class collision, forbidden desire, and visual depth that only 35mm can deliver. Metrograph's 35mm print is the only way to see this film tonight.

ratings.plot: A high-school boy in the early 1970s is given the chance to write a story for Rolling Stone magazine about an up-and-coming rock band as he accompanies them on their concert tour.

verdict.reason: Crowe's best film about the messy collision of fandom, fame, and growing up deserves the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes the 1970s rock aesthetic sing.

ratings.plot: A man who has struggled personally has conflicts with his upwardly mobile lawyer brother and well to-do fiancee and is reluctantly to be the best man at their wedding.

verdict.reason: Essential Burnett—a sharp, funny look at class and family told with real specificity. Film Forum's restoration brings out the precision of his 16mm cinematography.

ratings.plot: From writer-director Chris Marrs Piliero comes a psychological horror about the weaponization of deepfake technology – and the disintegration of truth in a digital-first culture. One app. One click. One life, ruined or ended. As a single piece of synthetic media metastasizes across feeds, the line between what happened and what was generated stops mattering. The film asks the only question left: if everyone will believe it, does the truth need you to?

verdict.reason: A sharp horror film about deepfakes and digital collapse that hits now. Piliero's premise cuts deeper than the gimmick—the real terror is how fast a lie spreads.

ratings.plot: An ostracized fisherwoman commissions the local basketmaker to weave her a husband, but when her wicker creation proves unexpectedly extraordinary, his presence ignites jealousy and upheaval that threatens their quiet village.

verdict.reason: A debut feature that trusts its absurd premise enough to let it breathe—the kind of original fantasy-comedy that belongs on a theater screen, not a laptop. Fischer and Wilson sustain the conceit without winking at it, and the Alamo's crowd-friendly room is the right place to discover something genuinely strange.

ratings.plot: The lives of a motherless boy, who is just starting to get interested in women, and his physically abused friend, who lives in poverty, are mixed with more or less innocent childhood experiences and challenges of a number of child...

verdict.reason: Truffaut's warmest film about childhood deserves the big screen. A 35mm print at Metrograph is the right way to see it.

movies.title: Once Upon a Time in China

ratings.plot: Legendary martial arts hero Wong Fei-Hung fights against foreign forces' plundering of China. When Aunt Yee arrives back from America, Wong Fei-Hung assumes the role of her protector.

verdict.reason: Essential action cinema from Hark Tsui at peak invention. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes the wire work and editing snap with clarity.

ratings.plot: A teenager at Rushmore Academy falls for a much older teacher and befriends a middle-aged industrialist. Later, he finds out that his love interest and his friend are having an affair, which prompts him to begin a vendetta.

verdict.reason: Anderson's deadpan comedy about adolescent obsession holds up perfectly on the big screen. Metrograph is showing the DCP restored, which sharpens every witty frame and musical cue.

ratings.plot: A cyborg assassin from the future attempts to find and kill a young woman who is destined to give birth to a warrior that will lead a resistance to save humankind from extinction.

verdict.reason: Essential action cinema—see it on the big screen at Metrograph. Cameron's control of pace and image design still dominates the room.

ratings.plot: An immigrant Romanian family living in Norway is subject to an investigation and faces the scrutiny of the local judicial system.

verdict.reason: Mungiu's first film in five years is a return to form—go see it on a big screen while it's here. The 146-minute runtime rewards patience, and the performance by the lead actor carries the weight of a family destroyed by bureaucracy.

ratings.plot: A cyborg from the future, identical to the one who failed to kill Sarah Connor, must now protect her ten-year-old son John from an even more advanced and powerful cyborg.

verdict.reason: Watch it. Cameron's action filmmaking from 1991 still holds up better than most blockbusters made since.

ratings.plot: Two death-obsessed sisters, outcasts in their suburban neighborhood, must deal with the tragic consequences when one of them is bitten by a deadly werewolf.

verdict.reason: A smart horror film that uses genre conventions to explore sisterhood and adolescent rage with real bite. Fawcett's direction gives the werewolf mythology genuine emotional weight.

ratings.plot: A determined taxi driver in Lagos forms an unexpected bond with a group of free-spirited women, leading her into a world of friendship and self-discovery despite the risks along the way.

verdict.reason: Olive Nwosu's debut feature earns a trip to Union Square for its sharp eye on Lagos life and female friendship. The 96-minute runtime lets the story breathe without overstaying.

ratings.plot: A vagabond swordsman is aided by a kunoichi and a spy in battling a demonic clan of killers led by a ghost from his past, who are bent on overthrowing the Tokugawa Shogunate.

verdict.reason: A landmark anime action film that still justifies the big screen. The hand-drawn animation and kinetic fight choreography demand theatrical impact.

ratings.plot: Rescued from abandonment and raised by the King and Queen, Oedipus is still haunted by a prophecy--he'll murder his father and marry his mother.

verdict.reason: Pasolini's radical reading of Greek tragedy demands a theater screen. The DCP restoration at Metrograph makes this a rare chance to see how he remade myth into lived nightmare.

ratings.plot: Two melancholic Hong Kong policemen fall in love: one with a mysterious female underworld figure, the other with a beautiful and ethereal waitress at a late-night restaurant he frequents.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai's neon-soaked romance belongs on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration catches every shimmer of light and color that defines his visual language.

ratings.plot: When Jonathan Harker rouses the ire of Count Dracula for accepting a job at the vampire's castle under false pretenses, his friend Dr. Van Helsing pursues the predatory villain.

verdict.reason: Fisher's 1958 vampire classic demands the big screen—the saturated Technicolor and sharp 35mm print at Metrograph make this essential. Lean 82 minutes of pure gothic atmosphere.

ratings.plot: John works with the PreCrime police which stop crimes before they take place, with the help of three 'PreCogs' who can foresee crimes. Events ensue when John finds himself framed for a future murder.

verdict.reason: Spielberg's sci-fi thriller holds up as smart action cinema with real ideas about free will. The Metrograph screening makes it worth the trip tonight.

ratings.plot: After his mother's sudden death, Socrates, a 15-year-old living on the margins of São Paulo's coast, must survive on his own while coming to terms with his grief.

verdict.reason: A rare screening of a lean, devastating debut at Metrograph that earns its 71 minutes through precise observation rather than sentiment. Moratto's camera stays close to his protagonist's face and hands, letting grief and survival register in glances and small gestures.

ratings.plot: In 2004, an ad director faces a turbulent Christmas weekend. In 2026, a filmmaker turns her story into a screenplay, blurring the lines between reality, fiction, and the people closest to him.

verdict.reason: Almodóvar playing with reality and fiction across two decades deserves a big screen. The layering of autobiography and invention is exactly what this director does best.

ratings.plot: A brave girl and her friends must escape a kids television show.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for a horror film that weaponizes children's TV against you. Casper Kelly mines genuine dread from a familiar format.

ratings.plot: A forgotten Peter Parker lives alone as a full-time Spider-Man until mounting pressure triggers a dangerous change and a powerful new enemy emerges.

verdict.reason: Cretton brings real weight to a Spider-Man origin that isolates Peter instead of crowding him with mentors. The 4DX format amplifies the action sequences across multiple theaters.

ratings.plot: A family's home becomes the center of paranormal activity that opens a doorway to the "other side." With help, they must cross over to get their daughter back.

verdict.reason: Essential horror that belongs on the biggest screen you can find. Hooper's practical effects and sound design create visceral scares that streaming can't replicate.

ratings.plot: The spirits of a deceased couple are harassed by an unbearable family that has moved into their home, and hire a malicious spirit to drive them out.

verdict.reason: Burton's deadpan comic timing and practical creature effects hold up on the big screen. Michael Keaton as the mischievous ghost steals every scene he's in.

ratings.plot: On July 27, 1986, Queen performed the largest-ever stadium concert at the Népstadion in Budapest in front of 80,000 ecstatic fans. The concert was part of the famed Magic Tour, which was the last time the band toured with lead singer Freddie Mercury. Now, this original concert film has been beautifully rescanned and remastered in 4K alongside a dynamic new audio mix, featuring many of Queen's favorite tracks – "Bohemian Rhapsody," "Crazy Little Thing Called Love," "I Want To Break Free," and "We Are The Champions." With three years to go before the fall of the Berlin Wall, this was the first Western rock concert performed in a stadium behind the then-Iron Curtain. It was of such significance to the Hungarian authorities and film industry that a group of the country's top film cameramen and technicians were brought together to film it for posterity.

verdict.reason: The 4K restoration of Queen's final tour with Freddie Mercury deserves the big screen and pristine sound. This is a historical document of a breakthrough moment—the first major Western rock concert behind the Iron Curtain—shot by Hungary's best cinematographers and now given the restoration it earned.

ratings.plot: Set high in the mountains, fall comes to an end and a family prepares for the long winter ahead.

ratings.plot: A businessman accidentally kills The Metal Fetishist, who gets his revenge by slowly turning the man into a grotesque hybrid of flesh and rusty metal.

ratings.plot: David Lynch cemented his reputation as an uncompromising visionary with BLUE VELVET, one of the most controversial films of the 1980s, burrowing beneath the surface of idyllic suburban America to reveal a sinister underworld of sex and violence. After stumbling upon a severed human ear, a young college student (Kyle MacLachlan) becomes obsessed with investigating its origins and gets entangled with a nightclub chanteuse (Isabella Rossellini) and her psychopathic lover (Dennis Hopper). A masterfully eerie, depraved psychosexual nightmare and one of the greatest films of the 1980s. “Frank Booth is the role Dennis Hopper was born and chemically mutated to own. Sometimes David Lynch can teeter too far into the absurdity for absurdity's sake, but BLUE VELVET remains perfectly balanced as it dives into the dark, bizarre underbelly of society that lurks just below the surface of suburbia. It is also worth noting that BLUE VELVET, when screened in the first month of operation at the original Alamo, was the movie that inspired our strict no-talking policy.” ( Tim League, Alamo Drafthouse founder)

verdict.reason: Lynch's masterpiece belongs on a big screen with an engaged crowd. Dennis Hopper's Frank Booth is unforgettable, and this screening at Alamo Drafthouse carries real history.

ratings.plot: One of the most derided movies of the 20th century is also one of its most spectacularly misunderstood. The odd-couple tag team of Dutch provocateur director Paul Verhoeven (ROBOCOP, ELLE) and Sleazoid-Hungarian-American writer Joe Eszterhas (FLASHDANCE, SLIVER) first came together with 1992's BASIC INSTINCT, and everyone, including the financial backers and the producer/distributors of this movie, assumed lightning would strike twice for the duo with 1995's SHOWGIRLS. Universally panned by critics upon its initial release, people found the multi-tap combo of inane dialogue, wild over-acting, and extreme obscenity and grotesquerie to be just too much. Then the "so-bad-it's-good" crowd sunk their hollow claws into the movie, claiming it as one of the "best worst" movies of all time. To be sure, yes, this is a movie in which Saved By the Bell 's Elizabeth Berkley sets fire to her TV-star image by grinding her pelvis on Kyle MacLachlan's lap until he simulates sexual climax while Gina Gershon watches. She shoves chips into her mouth and reminisces about her days of eating and enjoying "puppy chow," between bouts of trying to make it as a Las Vegas showgirl "goddess." The assumption that critics and chuckleheads alike have made are that a) Verhoeven and Eszterhas weren't trying to make something with humor (they were), and b) that the surface story is meant to be taken at face value (it's not). Verhoemie don't play that. SHOWGIRLS is a complicated, satirical masterpiece that tests the audience's limits of empathy and challenges some basic assumptions about American dreams of celebrity, pokes at the artificiality of Hollywood glitz and glamour, and shines a light on the misogyny and dehumanization inherent in the entertainment industry, all while keeping the audiences on their toes as they try to know whether they should laugh, cry, or scratch their heads because there are random interruptions by chimpanzees and the fiercest dancing ever committed to celluloid. (Laird Jimenez)

movies.title: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari w/ Invincible Czars

ratings.plot: It is difficult to imagine precisely what cinema would be without its most influential and memorable titles. THE CABINET OF DR. CALIGARI in particular stands out as one such notable title in the international canon that in its time and forever thereafter has been heralded as a masterpiece of its craft, the singular model for expressionist, black-and-white filmmaking. A landmark of horror filmmaking, its visual style is often copied or paid homage, and its remarkable twist ending has become all but a modern trope. Its long, haunting shadows and canted, dreamlike production design stay with viewers weeks, months, and years following an initial viewing. The film is credited for introducing the "twist" ending and inspired EDWARD SCISSORHANDS by Tim Burton, THE IMAGINARIUM OF DR. PARNASSUS by Terry Gilliam, and Martin Scorsese's SHUTTER ISLAND, all of which share many striking similarities to CALIGARI. "The first thing everyone notices and best remembers about THE CABINET OF DR. CALIGARI (1920) is the film's bizarre look. The actors inhabit a jagged landscape of sharp angles and tilted walls and windows, staircases climbing crazy diagonals, trees with spiky leaves, grass that looks like knives. These radical distortions immediately set the film apart from all earlier ones." – Roger Ebert, Chicago Sun-Times

verdict.reason: See the expressionist blueprint on the big screen with live music. The jagged set design and canted angles demand theatrical scale.

Hutter arrives at his destination safely and the Count is all too eager to buy the proposed property, especially after he sees a photo of Hutter's pretty young wife Ellen. Hutter nonetheless arrives home the same day as Orlok and the townsfolk begin to panic over the increasing number of deaths.

verdict.reason: See this foundational vampire film on the big screen with a live band that earned its reputation by understanding silent cinema's rhythmic hunger. Murnau's visual architecture—shadows as living things, composition as dread—demands theatrical space and the Invincible Czars provide the pulse that transforms viewing into ritual.
